subject: Copywriting
title: The Close: Ask for the Sale
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Close: Ask for the Sale.

hook.text: Many sales letters build desire perfectly—then forget to ask for the sale. The close must be direct: buy now.

buildup.text: The close restates the offer, adds urgency, and provides clear instructions. 'Click here,' 'Mail this card,' 'Call now.'

discovery.text: Adding a deadline to the close can double response. 'Offer expires Friday' creates action that 'Act now' alone can't.

twist.text: The PS line after the signature is the second close. It restates urgency or the guarantee.

climax.text: The best closes overcome the last objection: risk.

punchline.text: Ask for the sale directly. Add a deadline. Remove the risk.

quiz.question: What can adding a deadline to the close do?

details.summary: The close is where the sale happens — or doesn't. After pages of persuasion, the copy must explicitly ask for the order, summarize the offer, remind the reader of key benefits, and create final urgency. Many otherwise excellent letters fail because they don't close decisively.
details.whyItMatters: The most common copywriting failure is building a brilliant case but failing to ask for the sale clearly and confidently. A weak close wastes everything that came before it.
takeaways: Always ask explicitly for the order — never assume the reader will act unprompted
Summarize the complete offer including bonuses, guarantee, and price
Create final urgency without being manipulative

faq.question: What makes a strong close?
faq.answer: Summarize the offer clearly, restate the key benefit and guarantee, add a final urgency element, and make the action step unmistakably clear. Then add a P.S. — the second-most-read element after the headline — that reinforces the main benefit or adds one final persuasive point.

faq.question: Why is the P.S. so important in sales letters?
faq.answer: Eye-tracking studies show many readers scan the headline and then skip to the P.S. before reading the body. The P.S. gets disproportionate attention because it feels like an afterthought — a personal, informal addition — which makes it feel more honest and less 'salesy.'
